# Ivan Bohun - a self-hosted swarm

> This site is served from six ESP32-S3 microcontrollers in a 10-inch rack in
> a London flat, not from a cloud provider. Four "serving blades" share one
> immortal MAC address that the elected leader wears like a mask; the leader
> serves no pages itself - it load-balances every connection to its peers.
> Two observers never serve a byte and only witness the swarm and paint what
> they see on their own screens. Built by Kyrylo Novotarskyi, a Principal
> Engineer in London.

The page you are reading lives in flash memory, brotli-compressed, behind a
TLS 1.3 handshake that terminates on a 240 MHz microcontroller. There is no
origin server, no CDN, no external fonts, scripts or trackers. The whole
machine - four blades, two screens, a switch, three fans - draws about 22
watts.

## How it works

- **The mask**: a locally administered MAC address no factory ever issued. The
  elected leader writes it into its own Ethernet controller and claims a static
  IP. Lose that node and the next one writes the same address into itself, sends
  a gratuitous ARP so the switch relearns the port, and carries on answering.
- **The balancer is elected too**: the leader is a layer-4 TCP splicer. It
  never terminates TLS and never parses HTTP - it relays raw bytes to
  whichever blade has the fewest connections in flight, and that blade
  answers. Kill the leader and the next one takes both the mask and the
  balancing, in under four seconds.
- **Election**: the lowest-numbered candidate that is *actually serving* leads -
  alive on the radio is not enough, since a blade with a dead wire or a server
  still starting cannot answer anyone. No votes, no coordinator, no consensus
  protocol. Every node computes the same answer from the same heartbeats.
- **Off the wire**: leader election runs entirely over encrypted ESP-NOW radio,
  so choosing a leader costs the network switch nothing and survives the very
  failures it exists to handle.
- **Honest limits**: a fresh HTTPS connection costs a ~650 ms P-256
  handshake, 99% of the price of saying hello, so the fleet's measured
  ceiling is about 2.9-3.0 new connections per second with nobody dropped.
  Requests over a warm keep-alive connection return in 40-60 ms, roughly
  40-50 per second across the fleet; past ~100 per second the splicer's own
  wire becomes the limit. Offered more, it queues rather than collapses. All
  of this is stated plainly on the site rather than hidden.

## Who built it

Kyrylo Novotarskyi - Principal Engineer, London. Fifteen years in distributed
systems, performance engineering and reliability. Previously Pump.fun, Kobalt
Music Group, Deliveroo, HappyCar, ironSource, Sixt/DriveNow.

## Endpoints

- `/` - the page itself (brotli or gzip, ETagged)
- `/roster` - live JSON view of the swarm. **Please do not poll this.** It is
  live telemetry served by a microcontroller; crawling it consumes the capacity
  real visitors need. Deliberately contains no network addresses.

## Notes for machines

- Content is stable and changes only when new firmware is released. Honour the
  `ETag` and `Cache-Control` headers; a conditional request costs this hardware
  almost nothing while a full fetch costs it a great deal.
- There is no API, no pagination and nothing behind a login. What you see is all
  there is.
